subject: ENGLISH
title: Sentence Workshop
objective: Distinguish complete sentences from fragments and use capitals and end punctuation.
introduction: Maxine is fixing broken sentences! Help her spot complete sentences and add capitals and end marks.

vocabulary.definition: Marks like . ! ? that help us read clearly.
A group of words that tells a complete idea.
The part of a sentence that tells who or what.

activities.instruction: Watch how a complete sentence is built!
activities.content: A complete sentence expresses a complete thought and normally has a subject and predicate.

feedback.retry: Check for a subject, a verb, and a complete thought. 💪

activities.accessibilityAlternative: Text alternative: A complete sentence expresses a complete thought and normally has a subject and predicate.

activities.instruction: Tap each complete sentence and read it!

feedback.correct: Great! You found the examples for Sentence Workshop. 🔎
feedback.retry: Tap a complete sentence and notice who acts and what happens. 💪

activities.accessibilityAlternative: A numbered list of the same examples is available for keyboard and screen-reader use.

activities.instruction: Sort each card: is it a complete sentence or a fragment?

feedback.correct: Great! You sorted the examples using the Sentence Workshop clue. 🎉
feedback.retry: Sort complete thoughts away from word groups missing a subject or verb. 💪

activities.accessibilityAlternative: Tap an item and then tap a labeled category; dragging is optional.

feedback.correct: Correct: The bird builds a nest.
feedback.retry: Choose the option that names who acts and what the subject does. 💪

activities.accessibilityAlternative: All choices are visible text and selectable with TalkBack.

activities.instruction: Match each sentence to its subject!

feedback.correct: Great! You matched each example with its Sentence Workshop explanation. 🔗
feedback.retry: Match each sentence with the subject who or what acts. 💪

activities.accessibilityAlternative: A list-based matching control replaces drag gestures.

activities.instruction: Put the steps for writing a complete sentence in order!

steps: Put the capital letter and period in place.

feedback.correct: Great! You put the Sentence Workshop steps in order. 🎉
feedback.retry: Order the check: find the subject, find the verb, then add capitals and punctuation. 💪

activities.accessibilityAlternative: Up and down buttons provide an alternative to dragging.

items.prompt: Which one has a subject AND a verb?
items.explanation: “Maxine reads a book.” has a subject (Maxine) and a verb (reads), so it is a complete sentence. The other choices are only pieces of a sentence.

items.prompt: Which sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a period?

options.text: The turtle swims in the pond.

items.explanation: 'The turtle swims in the pond.' is a complete sentence that starts with a capital 'T' and ends with a period.

items.prompt: Which group of words is NOT a complete sentence?
items.explanation: “Under the chair” has no subject doing an action, so it is not a complete sentence. The other choices tell complete thoughts.
“The bird builds a nest.” has a subject (the bird) and a verb (builds). The other choices are fragments — they do not tell a complete idea.

items.prompt: Which group of words is a complete thought?
items.explanation: “Our class planted seeds.” tells who did it and what they did, so it is a complete thought. The other choices leave you waiting for more.
